Appendix A Dataset preparation

Excluded resources.

Some candidate resources were excluded on purpose: the French and German portions of the XLM-EMO training data, which are machine translations of Spanish tweets rather than native texts; EmoDIFT, a French corpus that has no joy class; and the French-emotion dataset on Hugging Face, which was generated synthetically by an LLM.

EmoEvent split.

The cleaned release of EmoEvent has numeric identifiers, so its official split was reconstructed by matching the texts against the official split files. Texts that could not be matched unambiguously (160 in English and 107 in Spanish) were assigned to no split.

Duplicates in BRIGHTER.

The BRIGHTER test split, built from tracks A and C of SemEval-2025 Task 11 [57], contains each of its 1,431 texts twice. Group resampling already accounts for this duplication in the confidence intervals, and recomputing all results with a single copy of each text changes no mean difference by more than 10−410^{-4}.

Appendix B Deviations from the analysis plan

The analysis followed a plan written before any paired test was computed. Four changes were made before the paired tests. First, the XLM-EMO matrix starts from the public xlm-emo-t checkpoint rather than from XLM-T base, because it is the only XLM-EMO run for which per-text predictions were stored. Second, invalid answers count as errors for all systems; re-querying the 9 invalid answers of GPT-6 Luna changes its mean score by less than 10−410^{-4}. Third, the H2 family includes the in-domain minus out-of-domain loss of each encoder. Fourth, the exploratory comparison with the public checkpoints used without training was added.

The following analyses were added after the first results and are reported as complementary: the random-effects meta-analysis for all pairs; for H1, the per-dataset equivalence tests, the alternative aggregations, the training-size moderator, the analysis of BRIGHTER without duplicates, the analysis without Universal Joy, the smallest equivalence margin δmin\delta_{\min} of each pair and the precision calculation; the inclusion of Qwen3.5-2B in the H1 family, which makes the Holm correction stricter for all pairs of the family (it was not added to the H2 family, because the plan included it only as the size-matched control for H3); the three tests of H4, which was descriptive in the plan, and the verdict rules of H3 and H4; and, for H2, the split of the sources by language, the comparison with the best source and the paired comparison of each out-of-domain encoder with its public checkpoint (Section 5.1); and the recalibration of encoders and decision models, with temperature scaling and with the removal of the class weights of the loss, its sensitivity analysis and the paired bootstrap of the calibration differences, whose comparisons were fixed in writing after the point estimates were known (Section 4.6). Five sets of runs were added between 28 October and 2 November 2026, after a review of the first version: label scoring of Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B and generative Qwen3.5-4B, the 2B models with instructions in English and in the language of the text, the three leading systems and Qwen3.5-4B with instructions in the language of the text, a controlled latency measurement and a second run of Jev and GPT-6 Luna (Section 3.6). They are complementary and do not change any verdict.

The plan numbered the hypotheses differently: H2 of this paper (out-of-domain) was H4 in the plan, H3 (decision models versus LLMs) was H2 and H4 (prompt sensitivity) was H3; the content of the hypotheses is unchanged. The plan was written after the descriptive macro-F1 of every system was known but before any paired test, and it fixed the pairs of each family; the three leading zero-shot systems were therefore identified on descriptive results.

A fifth hypothesis of the original plan, according to which an emotion-oriented starting checkpoint fine-tunes better than XLM-T base, was dropped, because the run that started from XLM-T base has no stored per-text predictions. The comparison between the two encoders is reported as exploratory (Table 22).

Appendix C Statistical details

Bootstrap.

Within each test set, groups of texts with the same normalised-text key are resampled with replacement, B=10,000B=10{,}000 times, with a fixed seed per test set (20261022 plus the alphabetical index of the test set). When a class is neither present in the gold labels nor predicted in a resample, it is left out of the macro average. In Universal Joy, where fear has 1 and 2 test texts, the average therefore covers three or four classes depending on the resample, and a single false fear prediction in a resample without gold fear sets that F1 to zero; this makes the per-dataset intervals of Universal Joy wide and asymmetric, which is one reason for the analysis without these two test sets (Section 4.2). Confidence intervals are percentile intervals. The two-sided bootstrap pp-value of an observed difference is p=2​(c+1)/(B+1)p=2(c+1)/(B+1), where cc is the number of resamples in which the difference has the sign opposite to the observed one; its minimum is therefore 0.0002. In a family of 10 pairs the smallest Holm-adjusted value is consequently 0.002, which explains why this value recurs in the tables.

Equivalence.

The TOST procedure rejects both one-sided null hypotheses Δ≤−δ\Delta\leq-\delta and Δ≥+δ\Delta\geq+\delta at level 0.05 exactly when the 90% CI lies within [−δ,+δ][-\delta,+\delta]. The one-sided pp-values reported in the text are the bootstrap proportions (c+1)/(B+1)(c+1)/(B+1), where cc is the number of resamples beyond each margin. As is standard, the TOST uses the unadjusted interval.

Random effects.

The model assumes that each test set has its own true difference; these true differences vary around a common mean with a between-dataset standard deviation τ\tau, and the observed difference on each test set adds sampling error to its true difference. For each pair, yjy_{j} is the observed difference on test set jj and vjv_{j} its bootstrap variance. The between-dataset variance τ2\tau^{2} is estimated by restricted maximum likelihood [58]. The CI of the mean difference uses the Hartung–Knapp standard error with a tt distribution on K−1K-1 degrees of freedom, where KK is the number of test sets [59, 60], and the 95% prediction interval uses a tt distribution on K−2K-2 degrees of freedom [37]. Heterogeneity is summarised by Cochran’s QQ and by I2I^{2} [54].

Precision of H1.

For each H1 pair of the three leading zero-shot systems, the stored resamples give the distribution of the unweighted mean difference over test sets. With test sets mm times larger, drawn from the same population, the deviations of this mean from its centre shrink by 1/m1/\sqrt{m}. For a true difference dd, we draw the estimate as dd plus a bootstrap deviation scaled by 1/m1/\sqrt{m}, build the 90% percentile CI with the scaled quantiles, and count the draws in which the CI lies within ±0.02\pm 0.02. The smallest mm with a share of at least 0.80 is 4.0–4.4 against tabularisaiin and 6.0–6.6 against XLM-EMOin for d=0d=0, and 9.0–11.2 and 13.4–22.6 at the observed differences. The calculation assumes that larger test sets would come from the same sources, and it is post hoc.

Permutation tests for H4.

The variant test checks whether the differences between variants are larger than expected if the variant had no effect, both over all test sets (Holm over the five systems) and for each test set (Holm over the 50 combinations of system and test set). The position test measures the share of answers given to the option shown in each of the four positions; under the Latin square, if the position does not matter, each position receives 25% of the answers. For each text, the four predictions of a system (one per variant) are permuted at random across the variants; the statistic is recomputed on each of P=5,000P=5{,}000 permutations, and p=(c+1)/(P+1)p=(c+1)/(P+1), where cc counts the permutations with a statistic at least as large as the observed one. For the variant effect the statistic is the mean SD of macro-F1 across variants; for position bias it is the sum, over the four positions, of the squared deviations of the share of answers from 25%.

Prompt and run components (complementary).

For Jev and GPT-6 Luna, each variant vv was run twice, with macro-F1 F1​vF_{1v} and F2​vF_{2v} on a test set. The variance due to the run is estimated as srun2=14​∑v(F1​v−F2​v)2/2s^{2}_{\text{run}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{v}(F_{1v}-F_{2v})^{2}/2, and the variance due to the prompt as sprompt2=max⁡(0,sbetween2−srun2/2)s^{2}_{\text{prompt}}=\max\bigl(0,\,s^{2}_{\text{between}}-s^{2}_{\text{run}}/2\bigr), where sbetween2s^{2}_{\text{between}} is the variance across the four variants of the mean of the two runs. The first factor 1/21/2 arises because the difference between two independent runs varies twice as much as a single run; the second because the mean of two runs keeps half of the run-to-run variance, which is removed so that only the variation due to the prompt remains. Both quantities are computed on each test set; their square roots, the two SDs, are averaged over test sets, and their CIs come from the same bootstrap resamples. The estimate assumes that the run-to-run variation is the same for the four variants; the two runs are about ten days apart, so any change in the service between them is counted as run-to-run variation; and with only two runs per variant both SDs are estimated imprecisely.

Calibration (complementary).

For a text ii, let pi​cp_{ic} be the probability assigned to class cc, y^i\hat{y}_{i} the predicted class and confi=pi​y^i\text{conf}_{i}=p_{i\hat{y}_{i}} its probability. The expected calibration error groups the texts into 15 equal-width bins of confi\text{conf}_{i} and is ECE=∑b(nb/n)​|accb−confb|\text{ECE}=\sum_{b}(n_{b}/n)\,|\text{acc}_{b}-\text{conf}_{b}|, where nbn_{b} is the number of texts in bin bb and accb\text{acc}_{b} and confb\text{conf}_{b} are their accuracy and mean confidence. The multiclass Brier score is 1n​∑i∑c(pi​c−yi​c)2\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\sum_{c}(p_{ic}-y_{ic})^{2}, with yi​c=1y_{ic}=1 for the gold class and 0 otherwise; it ranges from 0 to 2. Both are computed for each variant or model and averaged as macro-F1 is.

Class weights. The encoders were trained with weights wc=N/(4​nc)w_{c}=N/(4\,n_{c}) (Section 3.4); their effect is removed by dividing each probability by wcw_{c} and renormalising over the four classes, which is equivalent to subtracting log⁡wc\log w_{c} from the logits. The largest weight is 147, for fear in Universal Joy German.

Temperature scaling. The logits are recovered as zi​c=log⁡pi​cz_{ic}=\log p_{ic}, up to a constant per text that the softmax ignores; Jev and OpenAI Decisions round their probabilities to two decimals, so their probabilities of zero are replaced by 0.005, half the rounding unit, while the other systems never return a probability of zero. The recalibrated probabilities are softmax​(zi/T)\text{softmax}(z_{i}/T), where the calibration temperature TT is estimated separately for each model or variant and test set by minimising the log-loss. Because predictions on the validation splits were not stored, each test set is split at random into two halves, with groups of identical texts kept together: TT is estimated on one half and applied to the other, and vice versa, and ECE and Brier are computed on the held-out halves. Temperature scaling does not change the predicted class.

Sensitivity. Over 200 random splits into halves, the 2.5–97.5% range of the mean expected calibration error is 0.043–0.053 for Jev, 0.037–0.046 for OpenAI Decisions, 0.035–0.042 for Strands Decider 2B, 0.056–0.060 and 0.040–0.046 for label-scored Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B, 0.046–0.058 for the encoders in-domain and 0.057–0.065 out of domain, so that Strands Decider 2B remains better calibrated than label-scored Qwen3.5-2B. With probabilities of zero replaced by 0.001, 0.0025 or 0.01 instead of 0.005, the recalibrated expected calibration error is 0.038–0.051 for Jev and 0.037–0.047 for OpenAI Decisions. For the encoders out of domain, a calibration temperature estimated on the in-domain test set of the same model, which needs no labels from the target domain (mean 2.1), gives 0.120 for tabularisai and 0.101 for XLM-EMO.

Bootstrap of the differences. The comparisons (Strands Decider 2B against the two label-scored Qwen models; each decision model against each encoder, in-domain and out of domain), the measures and the decision rule were written down on 4 November 2026, after the point estimates were known and before any interval was computed. The resamples are those of the paired group bootstrap of macro-F1 (B=10,000B=10{,}000); in every resample, ECE and Brier are recomputed for every model or variant, averaged as above, and, for the recalibrated probabilities, the calibration temperature is re-estimated on the resampled texts of each half, on a grid of log⁡T\log T from −3-3 to 3 in steps of 0.025. Brier differences are tested with the bootstrap pp-value and Holm’s correction over the 28 tests (14 comparisons, as returned and recalibrated); the ECE, which depends on the binning, receives 95% percentile intervals only. The plan also foresaw intervals for the ECE of each system, which are not reported: the ECE of a resample is biased upwards, so that for most systems the bootstrap distribution lies above the estimate; in the differences between two systems this bias largely cancels. Results are in Table 27.

Appendix D Prompt variants

Table 14 lists the four question variants and the order in which the options were presented in each of them, and Table 15 the descriptions of the four classes, identical in all variants. The option keys (joy, sadness, anger, fear) are in English in every condition.

What each system receives.

Jev and OpenAI Decisions receive the question, the four options with their descriptions in the order of the variant, and the text preceded by the label Testo (“Text”). GPT-6 Luna and Qwen3.5-2B receive a single prompt: the question; the sentence Scegli una sola classe tra le seguenti: (“Choose exactly one of the following classes:”); one line “- class: description” per option, in the order of the variant; the sentence Rispondi solo con il nome della classe (joy, sadness, anger oppure fear), senza altre parole. (“Answer only with the class name (joy, sadness, anger or fear), no other words.”), with the classes in the order of the variant; and the text after Testo:. Label scoring uses the same prompt. Strands Decider 2B receives the question, the descriptions and the text with its label, and builds the rest of its prompt internally.

Translations.

For the complementary runs, the question, the class descriptions and the sentences above were translated into English, German, Spanish and French with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and checked by one of the authors; they were not reviewed by native speakers. The texts in all five languages are released with the code; Tables 14 and 15 give the English version.

Appendix F Compute and reproducibility

All systems were run on AWS SageMaker. The calls to the three API-based systems were made from CPU instances, Strands Decider 2B and Qwen3.5-2B ran on single GPUs one request at a time, and the fine-tuned encoders were evaluated on T4 GPUs in batches of 32 texts. The zero-shot suite (5 systems, 4 variants, 12,633 texts) was run on 19 October 2026 and took 3 h 18 min of wall-clock time with the systems running in parallel and cost USD 7.98 of SageMaker compute, to which the API fees, billed separately, must be added. Fine-tuning 30 tabularisai models cost USD 10.22 and fine-tuning 24 XLM-EMO models USD 6.37, with the models trained in series on single GPUs (L4, L40S or A10G). The open zero-shot models were used at the following Hugging Face commits: 15852e8c1636 for Qwen3.5-2B, 851bf6e806ef for Qwen3.5-4B and 2b52a6235c1b for Strands Decider 2B. Once trained, the encoders classify a text in a median of 2.5–3.3 ms on a T4 GPU in batches of 32. Table 28 gives the median, mean and 95th percentile of the latency of every system.

The complementary runs of 28 October to 2 November 2026 cost about USD 20 of SageMaker compute for the three local models and an estimated USD 3.5 of API fees. All statistics were computed locally from the stored predictions. The bootstrap seeds are 20261022 plus the alphabetical index of the test set. The per-text predictions of every system and the statistical scripts will be released in a public repository upon publication of this article.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
